newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan bid for growth seen as high-stake gamble. [CORRECTED 10:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Pakistan bid for growth seen as high-stake gamble. [CORRECTED 10:40 GMT]

text.p: Pakistan's planned economic reforms are a gamble that could reap rich rewards or go awry if fiscal discipline cracks, analysts said on Wednesday.
President Farooq Leghari cast a harsh spotlight on his country's plight in a speech to both houses of parliament.
"The condition of the economy is very fragile," he said on Wednesday, adding that spending outstripped revenue and the national debt now equalled 84 percent of national income.
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif is to unveil a sweeping economic reform package in the next day or two that will slash taxes, tariffs and public spending to stimulate growth and exports.
The economic package follows the collapse of an International Monetary Fund standby loan, effectively suspended last week because Pakistan could not meet agreed targets.
The IMF has agreed to continue monitoring the economy and possibly start talks on a medium-term enhanced structural adjustment facility (ESAF) programme later in the year.
"The low level of foreign exchange reserves poses the biggest risk to a 'growing out of problems' policy," said a report by Jardine Fleming Pakistan, a Karachi securities house.
"A policy of credit growth and incentives to kick-start the sick industry is bound to fuel inflation," it added.
An Islamabad-based analyst said market reaction would be critical to the fate of the economy. "If they take it as a break with the IMF and start capital flight, there is a problem."

Expected tax and tariff cuts in Sharif's package implied certain revenue losses, he said, whereas anticipated revenue benefits from higher economic growth and efforts to widen the tax and tariff base were harder to predict.

"The revenue shortfall this year is likely to exceed 30 billion rupees ($746 million)," said the analyst, who asked not to be named. Domestic bank borrowing was now around 80 billion rupees, against a whole-year target of 20 billion, he added.

The IMF had wanted Pakistan to cut its deficit to four percent of gross domestic product in fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) from 6.3 percent the previous year, but analysts now say this year's gap could be at least 5.5 percent.

Jardine Fleming said that with defence spending and debt servicing consuming 76 percent of gross revenue receipts and 107 percent of total taxes, Pakistan might have no option but to raise revenue by growth-oriented supply side measures.
"Raising revenue, through direct and indirect taxation, by boosting supply makes sense in the context of Pakistan's lop-sided revenue-expense equation," it said.
But increasing revenue through inflationary measures could lead to steeper depreciation of the rupee and thus increase the import bill and put pressure on reserves, it added.
The report said rupee depreciation against the dollar was already forecast at 14 percent (corrects from 17.46 percent) in 1997/98.
Jardine Fleming said the risk would be worth running if Pakistan had around $2 billion in liquid reserves, but described this as "a difficult feat to acomplish without IMF tutelage".
Liquid foreign reserves are now about $1.13 billion and debt payments of about $1 billion are due in April-June.

The Islamabad-based analyst said the economy could turn around quickly if the right policies were in place, but added that unless the government maintained strict fiscal and monetary discipline, its programme could run into trouble.
"If the demand management is not strong enough, the imbalances can widen even further and make the macro-economic situation much more fragile," he said.
